topic: The composition and evolution of the Earth's atmosphere
subject: chemistry

items.q: For roughly how long have the proportions of the different gases in the atmosphere been much the same as they are today?
items.correct: About 200 million years
items.misconception: About 4.6 billion years
items.why: 4.6 billion years is the figure students meet most often, so it is attached to every fact about the Earth. The idea that air itself has a history is unfamiliar. 4.6 billion years is the age of the Earth and the reason evidence about the early atmosphere is limited. The present proportions have only held for the last 200 million years.
items.random_wrong: About 2.7 billion years

items.q: Which of these best describes the proportions of the two main gases in the atmosphere today?
items.correct: About 80% nitrogen, about 20% oxygen
items.misconception: About 80% oxygen and about 20% nitrogen
items.why: Oxygen is the gas students hear about constantly – in breathing, burning and rusting – so importance is mistaken for abundance. Nitrogen is rarely mentioned because it is unreactive. Importance is not the same as abundance. Nitrogen is about 80% of the air and oxygen about 20%; oxygen matters to us because of what it does, not because there is a lot of it.
items.random_wrong: About 80% nitrogen, 20% carbon dioxide

items.q: Which statement about carbon dioxide, water vapour and the noble gases in the air today is correct?
items.correct: Together they make up a small part.
items.misconception: Together they make up about one fifth.
items.why: Carbon dioxide dominates discussion of climate change and of respiration, and pie charts in textbooks often exaggerate its slice so it can be seen at all. Nitrogen (about 80%) and oxygen (about 20%) account for nearly all of the air. Carbon dioxide, water vapour and the noble gases together make up only the small remaining proportion.
items.random_wrong: Carbon dioxide alone makes up about 20%.

items.q: Why is the evidence about the Earth's early atmosphere limited?
items.correct: The time scale involved is 4.6 billion years.
items.misconception: Instruments to measure it have not been built.
items.why: Students trust that modern instruments can measure anything, and do not distinguish between measuring something that exists now and reconstructing something that vanished billions of years ago. No sample of the early atmosphere survives. Because of the time scale of 4.6 billion years the evidence is limited and indirect, so ideas about the early atmosphere remain theories.
items.random_wrong: There is no evidence about it left at all.

items.q: Theories about the Earth's early atmosphere have changed and developed over time. What does this best show?
items.correct: Explanations are revised when new evidence appears.
items.misconception: The earlier scientists were careless in their own research.
items.why: Students expect science to deliver fixed facts, so revision looks like failure rather than the normal way scientific explanations improve. Changing a theory when new evidence appears is exactly how science is supposed to work. Earlier scientists were reasoning from the evidence they had; more evidence produced a better explanation.
items.random_wrong: Evidence about the early atmosphere is now complete.

items.q: According to the theory in the specification, what was the Earth's atmosphere like at the start of its first billion years?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide, with little or no oxygen
items.misconception: Oxygen, with little or no carbon dioxide
items.why: Students reason backwards from the present: because life needs oxygen now, they assume oxygen has always been there, and they do not picture a world without living things. The oxygen came later. It was produced by algae from about 2.7 billion years ago and then by plants; at the start there was little or no oxygen gas, which is why only organisms that did not need oxygen could exist.
items.random_wrong: Nitrogen, with little or no carbon dioxide

items.q: Scientists use the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today as a model for the Earth's early atmosphere. Why?
items.correct: They consist mainly of carbon dioxide today.
items.misconception: They consist of nitrogen and oxygen.
items.why: Students treat today's composition as what 'air' means by definition, and so project about 80% nitrogen and about 20% oxygen back to the beginning. The early atmosphere was mainly carbon dioxide. Nitrogen built up gradually from volcanic activity and oxygen only appeared once algae began to photosynthesise about 2.7 billion years ago.
items.random_wrong: They have the same atmosphere as us.

items.q: According to the theory in the specification, how did the Earth's oceans form?
items.correct: Water vapour from volcanoes condensed.
items.misconception: Water vapour from photosynthesis condensed.
items.why: Water appears in both the photosynthesis and respiration equations, so students reach for a biological source for water instead of a volcanic one. In the photosynthesis equation water is a reactant, not a product. The ocean water came from water vapour released by intense volcanic activity, which condensed as the Earth cooled.
items.random_wrong: The oceans were there when Earth formed.

items.q: Where did the nitrogen in the Earth's atmosphere come from?
items.correct: Volcanoes produced it and it built up slowly.
items.misconception: Algae produced it during photosynthesis.
items.why: Having learned that algae and plants produced the oxygen, students apply the same explanation to the other major gas. Nitrogen came from volcanoes and built up gradually because it is unreactive and is not readily removed. Only the oxygen is attributed to algae and plants.
items.random_wrong: It was present when the Earth first formed.

items.q: Which pair of gases may have been present in small proportions in the Earth's early atmosphere?
items.correct: Methane and ammonia
items.misconception: Methane and oxygen
items.why: Students reason backwards from the present: because life needs oxygen now, they assume oxygen has always been there, and they do not picture a world without living things. The oxygen came later. It was produced by algae from about 2.7 billion years ago and then by plants; at the start there was little or no oxygen gas, which is why only organisms that did not need oxygen could exist.
items.random_wrong: Ammonia and argon

items.q: When the oceans formed, how was carbon dioxide removed from the atmosphere?
items.correct: It dissolved and carbonates were precipitated.
items.misconception: Sunlight broke it down into carbon and oxygen.
items.why: Students know sunlight is involved in producing oxygen and know carbon dioxide contains oxygen, and combine the two into a purely physical process with no organisms in it. The oxygen was produced by living organisms: algae from about 2.7 billion years ago, and later plants, by photosynthesis, 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2.
items.random_wrong: It was used up by animals during respiration.

items.q: A scientist argues that because Mars and Venus have atmospheres of mainly carbon dioxide, the Earth's early atmosphere was certainly the same. What is the main weakness of this argument?
items.correct: Other planets may have developed in different ways.
items.misconception: Data sent back by space probes are never reliable.
items.why: Students read 'limited' as 'none', and conclude that if certainty is impossible then all ideas are equal and evaluation is pointless. Limited evidence is not zero evidence. Evidence such as the composition of the atmospheres of Mars and Venus, and the carbonate sediments in ancient rocks, supports some explanations better than others, so theories can still be evaluated.
items.random_wrong: Ideas about the distant past can never be tested.

items.q: Which equation represents photosynthesis, as given in the specification?
items.why: Photosynthesis and respiration have the same substances on opposite sides of the equation, and students who have memorised only the substances lose track of which side each is on. In photosynthesis carbon dioxide and water are the reactants and glucose and oxygen the products: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2. Photosynthesis therefore removes carbon dioxide and releases oxygen.

items.q: Which process produced the oxygen that is now in the Earth's atmosphere?
items.correct: Photosynthesis by algae and plants
items.misconception: Respiration by early algae and plants
items.why: Photosynthesis and respiration have the same substances on opposite sides of the equation, and students who have memorised only the substances lose track of which side each is on. In photosynthesis carbon dioxide and water are the reactants and glucose and oxygen the products: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2. Photosynthesis therefore removes carbon dioxide and releases oxygen.
items.random_wrong: Volcanic activity on the early Earth

items.q: About how long ago did algae first produce oxygen?
items.correct: About 2.7 billion years ago
items.misconception: About 4.6 billion years ago
items.why: 4.6 billion years is the figure students meet most often, so it is attached to every fact about the Earth. The idea that air itself has a history is unfamiliar. 4.6 billion years is the age of the Earth and the reason evidence about the early atmosphere is limited. The present proportions have only held for the last 200 million years.
items.random_wrong: About 200 million years ago

items.q: Which sequence matches the way the specification describes the rise of oxygen?
items.correct: Algae made oxygen, then plants evolved, then animals
items.misconception: Plants evolved, then algae made oxygen, then animals
items.why: Plants are the familiar photosynthesising organisms, so students assume they were the original ones and treat algae as a minor afterthought. Algae were first, producing oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago. Plants evolved over the following billion years, and the percentage of oxygen increased to a level that enabled animals to evolve.
items.random_wrong: Animals evolved, then algae made oxygen, then plants

items.q: What effect did the spread of algae and plants have on the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
items.correct: It decreased, because photosynthesis uses it.
items.misconception: It increased, because photosynthesis makes it.
items.why: Photosynthesis and respiration have the same substances on opposite sides of the equation, and students who have memorised only the substances lose track of which side each is on. In photosynthesis carbon dioxide and water are the reactants and glucose and oxygen the products: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2. Photosynthesis therefore removes carbon dioxide and releases oxygen.
items.random_wrong: It decreased, because respiration removes it.

items.q: Apart from photosynthesis, what else decreased the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
items.correct: Carbon became locked in rocks and fossil fuels.
items.misconception: Burning fossil fuels took it out of the air.
items.why: Students meet fossil fuels almost exclusively as something that is burned, so the formation of the fuel, which locked carbon away, is never considered. Two separate events. When fossil fuels formed, carbon taken from the air by living organisms was buried and locked away, decreasing carbon dioxide. Burning them now returns that carbon to the atmosphere.
items.random_wrong: Carbon dioxide escaped from Earth into space.

items.q: How were deposits of limestone formed?
items.correct: From shells and skeletons of marine organisms
items.misconception: From thick deposits of buried plant material
items.why: All four are taught together as carbon stores formed by burial over millions of years, and the shared process makes the different starting materials feel interchangeable. The starting material is the point of difference. Shells and skeletons give limestone, thick plant deposits give coal, and plankton buried in mud give crude oil and natural gas.
items.random_wrong: From volcanic ash settling onto the sea bed

items.q: Crude oil and natural gas were formed from the remains of which organisms?
items.correct: Plankton buried in mud on the sea floor
items.misconception: Thick deposits of buried plant material
items.why: All four are taught together as carbon stores formed by burial over millions of years, and the shared process makes the different starting materials feel interchangeable. The starting material is the point of difference. Shells and skeletons give limestone, thick plant deposits give coal, and plankton buried in mud give crude oil and natural gas.
items.random_wrong: Remains of dinosaurs buried in the rock

items.q: Coal is a sedimentary rock. What was it formed from?
items.correct: Thick deposits of plant material
items.misconception: Plankton buried in sea-bed mud
items.why: All four are taught together as carbon stores formed by burial over millions of years, and the shared process makes the different starting materials feel interchangeable. The starting material is the point of difference. Shells and skeletons give limestone, thick plant deposits give coal, and plankton buried in mud give crude oil and natural gas.
items.random_wrong: Remains of buried land animals

items.q: Which pair of changes describes how the Earth's atmosphere changed over most of its history?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide fell and oxygen rose
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide rose and oxygen fell
items.why: Students reason backwards from the present: because life needs oxygen now, they assume oxygen has always been there, and they do not picture a world without living things. The oxygen came later. It was produced by algae from about 2.7 billion years ago and then by plants; at the start there was little or no oxygen gas, which is why only organisms that did not need oxygen could exist.
items.random_wrong: Both carbon dioxide and oxygen rose

items.q: How much of the air is made up of the noble gases?
items.correct: The noble gases are among the various other gases present in only small proportions.
items.misconception: The noble gases are a whole group of the periodic table, so together they must make up a large share of the air.
items.why: A group of eight elements sounds substantial, and argon is often singled out in diagrams of the air, which makes it look more abundant than it is. The number of elements in a group says nothing about their abundance. The noble gases in the air are part of the small proportion of other gases left after about 80% nitrogen and about 20% oxygen.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happened about 2.7 billion years ago?
items.correct: Algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago, and soon after this oxygen appeared in the atmosphere.
items.misconception: About 2.7 billion years ago the atmosphere reached the composition it has today.
items.why: Students collect the dates in this topic without attaching each one to its event, so 2.7 billion years is used as a general 'the air became normal' marker. 2.7 billion years ago is when algae first produced oxygen. The percentage of oxygen then rose gradually over the next billion years; the present proportions have only held for the last 200 million years.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which process decreased the carbon dioxide in the early atmosphere?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide decreased through dissolving in the oceans and being precipitated as carbonates, through photosynthesis, and through the formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels.
items.misconception: Respiration is what took the carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere.
items.why: Respiration is the process students associate most strongly with carbon dioxide, and they do not check the direction: respiration releases carbon dioxide, it does not remove it. Respiration releases carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide was removed by dissolving in the oceans and precipitating as carbonates, by photosynthesis, and by burial as sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Mars and Venus have carbon dioxide atmospheres. What does that show?
items.correct: The Earth's early atmosphere may have been like the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today, consisting of mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen gas.
items.misconception: Because Mars and Venus have carbon dioxide atmospheres, we know for certain the early Earth did too.
items.why: A comparison that supports an idea is easily read as proof of it, especially when the specification's wording 'may have been' is skimmed over. Mars and Venus provide supporting evidence, not proof. They are different planets that may have developed differently, so the comparison makes the theory plausible without confirming it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Were the Earth's oceans and its present gases there from the start?
items.correct: The gases of the early atmosphere were released by volcanic activity, and the oceans formed when volcanic water vapour condensed.
items.misconception: The oceans and the gases were all there from the moment the Earth formed.
items.why: Students picture the Earth forming complete, like a finished model, rather than as a body whose surface and atmosphere developed over the first billion years. During the first billion years intense volcanic activity released the gases that formed the early atmosphere, along with the water vapour that condensed to form the oceans.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Did volcanoes produce all the gases in today's atmosphere?
items.correct: Volcanoes released the gases of the early atmosphere, including carbon dioxide and nitrogen; the oxygen came from photosynthesis by algae and plants.
items.misconception: Volcanoes released every gas in the air, so the oxygen came from volcanoes too.
items.why: Once students learn that volcanic activity formed the early atmosphere, they extend it to the whole of the modern atmosphere and overlook the biological origin of oxygen. Volcanic gases account for the carbon dioxide, the nitrogen and possibly the methane and ammonia. The oxygen now in the atmosphere was produced by algae and plants through photosynthesis.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why could animals only evolve when they did?
items.correct: Over the billion years after algae appeared, plants evolved and the percentage of oxygen gradually increased to a level that enabled animals to evolve.
items.misconception: Animals were around before there was much oxygen, and the oxygen built up around them.
items.why: Students think of the fossil record as a story about animals, so animals are placed at the beginning rather than as latecomers who depended on oxygen already being present. Oxygen came first. Algae produced it from about 2.7 billion years ago and plants added to it over the next billion years, until the percentage of oxygen reached a level that enabled animals to evolve.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happened to the carbon dioxide that left the early atmosphere?
items.correct: It dissolved in the oceans and was precipitated as carbonate sediments, was used in photosynthesis, and was locked into sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels.
items.misconception: The carbon dioxide escaped from the Earth into space.
items.why: Students who cannot name a chemical sink for the gas reach for the only other destination they can picture, and gas escaping upwards feels intuitive. The carbon did not leave the planet; it moved into the oceans, into carbonate sediments, into sedimentary rocks such as limestone, and into fossil fuels. Each of these is a store of carbon on Earth.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How did limestone form?
items.correct: Limestone formed from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms, which are made of calcium carbonate.
items.misconception: Limestone is made from volcanic material that settled and hardened into rock.
items.why: Volcanic activity dominates the early part of this topic, so students use it to explain rock formation generally and do not separate sedimentary rock from igneous rock. Limestone is a sedimentary rock. It formed from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms deposited on the sea bed, which is how carbon from the atmosphere became locked into rock.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What was crude oil formed from?
items.correct: Crude oil and natural gas were formed from plankton, that is, marine organisms buried in mud.
items.misconception: Crude oil was formed from the remains of dinosaurs.
items.why: The phrase 'fossil fuel' plus popular images of dinosaur-era swamps produce a memorable but wrong story that students rarely question. Crude oil and natural gas formed from plankton – microscopic marine organisms – buried in mud on the sea bed and altered over millions of years by heat and pressure.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What was coal formed from?
items.correct: Coal was formed from thick deposits of plant material.
items.misconception: Coal formed from the buried bodies of land animals.
items.why: Once oil has been attached to animal remains, coal is assumed to have an animal origin too, since both are fossil fuels formed by burial. Coal formed from thick deposits of plant material that were buried and compressed over millions of years, which is why coal is essentially carbon that plants had taken from the atmosphere.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the photosynthesis equation need to balance?
items.correct: The equation is 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2, which balances: 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 18 oxygen atoms on each side.
items.misconception: As long as the right substances are on the right sides, the numbers in front do not really matter.
items.why: Students treat the equation as a word summary written in symbols, so the big numbers look decorative rather than as a statement that atoms are conserved. Atoms are not created or destroyed, so the numbers must make each element balance. 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 3O2 is wrong because oxygen atoms do not balance.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.9.1 The composition and evolution of the Earth's atmosphere
